explanations.At FDA's Recommendation: The manufacturer recalled it at the FDA's request. The FDA's page for this recall has the specific reason.
explanations.CGMP Deviations: The factory broke a manufacturing or record-keeping rule. This is often about paperwork or process, not a known problem with the product itself — but the FDA recalls it to be safe.
explanations.Child-Resistant Packaging Failure: The packaging doesn't meet a safety rule — often that the cap isn't child-resistant. The medicine itself is usually unaffected.
explanations.Counterfeit: The product may be counterfeit or tampered with.
explanations.Defective Container: The bottle, cartridge, or dispenser is faulty — it may leak, not seal properly, or not dispense correctly.
explanations.Discoloration: The product changed in appearance — discoloration or crystals — which can mean it's degrading.
explanations.Failed Dissolution Specifications: Tablets may not dissolve properly, so the medication may be released too slowly or unevenly.
explanations.Failed Impurities/Degradation Specificat: Testing found the medication breaking down, or an impurity, beyond the limit the FDA allows.
explanations.Failed Stability Specifications: The product may lose strength before its expiration date.
explanations.Failed Tablet/Capsule Specifications: im: The marking stamped on the tablets or capsules is wrong or missing, so they could be confused with another medication.
explanations.Failed USP Dissolution Test Requirements: Tablets may not dissolve properly, so the medication may be released too slowly or unevenly.
explanations.Labeling: Label Error on Declared Streng: The label on some packages is wrong — it may name a different drug, strength, or count than what's inside.
explanations.Lack of Assurance of Sterility: The manufacturer couldn't show that its process was properly controlled. Often a paperwork or process issue rather than a known problem with the product.
explanations.Lack of Processing Controls: The manufacturer couldn't show that its process was properly controlled. Often a paperwork or process issue rather than a known problem with the product.
explanations.Marketed Without an Approved NDA/ANDA: The product was sold without FDA approval or outside what its approval allows.
explanations.Presence of Foreign Tablets/Capsules: Some bottles may contain a different medication than the label says.
explanations.Presence of Nitrosamine Impurity (NDMA): Testing found a nitrosamine impurity above the level the FDA allows. The amount matters, and the FDA's page for this recall has the details.
explanations.Presence of Particulate Matter: Small particles (like glass or fibers) were found in the product. Most serious for injections.
explanations.Product Mix-Up: Some bottles may contain a different medication than the label says.
explanations.Subpotent Drug: Some doses may be weaker than the label says, so they may not work as expected.
explanations.Superpotent Drug: Some doses may be stronger than the label says.
explanations.Temperature Excursion During Shipping: The product was exposed to temperatures outside its safe range during storage or shipping.

whatToDo.Class I: Don't take another dose until you've talked to your pharmacist — call today, or call the number on the recall. Don't throw the bottle away yet; they may want the lot number.
whatToDo.Class II: Don't stop taking it on your own. Check the lot number against your bottle, and call or visit your pharmacist — they can replace it if it's affected.
whatToDo.Class III: This kind of recall rarely affects your health. Mention it at your next refill, or ask your pharmacist if you're unsure.
whatToDo.Unclassified: Don't stop taking a medication on your own. Take your bottle to your pharmacist, or call them, and ask whether it's part of this recall and what to do next.
